summary: Tipaza, the capital of Algeria's Tipaza Province, was known as Tipasa under Roman rule and developed from a Punic trading-post into a military colony and Christian hub with three basilicas. The modern town was founded in 1857, has nearly 30,000 inhabitants, and attracts tourists principally through its ancient ruins and sandy littoral.

coreControversy.regulatoryOrHistoricalPrecedent: An old Punic trading-post, Tipasa was conquered by Ancient Rome and converted by Claudius into a military colony for the conquest of the kingdoms of Mauretania; it subsequently became a municipium called Colonia Aelia Tipasensis. Destruction by the Vandals in 430 CE was followed by Byzantine reconstruction one century later and demolition by Umayyad forces at the end of the seventh century.

hiddenCatchesAndLimits: The ancient population of 20,000 inhabitants in the fourth century is attributed to Stéphane Gsell; the modern population is described as nearly 30,000 inhabitants.
The transmitter's reported return to broadcasting at 252 kHz followed an outage beginning March 17, 2014.
The modern town's founding in 1857 is distinct from the history of ancient Tipasa and its successive destruction and reconstruction.

fitAdvice: Tipaza's tourism importance rests principally on the ruins of ancient Tipasa, alongside its sandy littoral.
Tipaza and its surroundings are home to the Chenoua people, described as the largest Berber-speaking group of western Algeria; the majority of the Bouriba family also reside in the area.
The nearby transmitter carries French language Channel 3 programs on 252 kHz, reaching many parts of Europe.
